note.note:
Consult Summary:
- Adult patient (discrepancy in recorded DOB noted) with ~1 week of sore throat progressing to dry cough, now with exertional shortness of breath, intermittent wheeze and chest discomfort; clinician’s working impression: likely viral upper respiratory infection with reactive bronchitic component; symptomatic treatment and sick note provided.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Sore throat beginning ~7 days ago, followed 1–2 days later by a dry, non-productive cough.
  - Shortness of breath began ~3–4 days ago, worse with exertion (walking/exercise) but not at rest.
  - Patient reports some wheeze and some chest pain.
- Timeline / progression:
  - Sore throat first (about last week), cough began within 1–2 days, breathlessness started ~3–4 days ago.
  - Symptoms fluctuating (improved then worse, intermittent), not steadily progressive; initial fever for first ~3 days then resolved.
  - Patient has missed work for 2–4 days this week; requests additional sick note.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Breathlessness worse with exertion; cough similar day and night (not nocturnal).
  - Rest, fluids, and paracetamol recommended by clinician (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Associated symptoms:
  - Transient fever (first ~3 days), intermittent headache, decreased appetite; no weight loss reported.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No productive cough, no hemoptysis, no nasal congestion/rhinorrhea, no recent significant travel outside Europe, no known asbestos exposure, no prior asthma history, no leg swelling reported.

Past Medical History:
- Patient reports no chronic medical conditions.
- Explicit denial of a history of asthma.

Medications:
- Current/recent medications: None reported.
- Treatments recommended in consult: Paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies: Allergy to peanuts (food).

Social History:
- Born in the U.S.; moved to the U.K. ~12 years ago.
- Recent travel only within Europe.
- Minimal prior smoking (“once or twice in Amsterdam”), otherwise non-smoker.
- Works (requested sick note for time off); specific occupation not documented.
- No reported illicit drug use or significant alcohol history documented.

Family History:
- Mother had lung cancer.
- No other family illnesses reported.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: No formal exam documented. Patient reports no palpable neck lumps. Otherwise “Not recorded.”

Investigations:
- No tests, imaging, or labs were ordered or reported during this consultation.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Most likely acute viral upper respiratory infection (viral pharyngitis with viral bronchitic/reactive airway component) causing sore throat, dry cough and exertional dyspnea; clinician expects improvement in several days and provided symptomatic care and a sick note.
- DDx Integration (brief):
  - 1) Acute viral URI with viral bronchitis — aligned with transcript and DDx as highest likelihood: supporting — sore throat → dry cough, transient fever, fluctuating one-week course; opposing — wheeze/exertional dyspnea could reflect lower tract involvement but can occur with viral bronchitis.
  - 2) Viral-induced reactive airways disease / new-onset asthma — medium likelihood per DDx: supporting — new wheeze and exertional dyspnea after viral prodrome; opposing — patient denies prior asthma and no objective exam/peak flow documented.
  - 3) Atypical (community-acquired) pneumonia — lower likelihood per DDx: supporting — progression to chest discomfort and dyspnea; opposing — absence of persistent high fever, productive cough, or focal findings and patient remains ambulatory.
- Issue 1: Acute viral upper respiratory infection / viral bronchitis
  - Assessment: Clinical course consistent with viral pharyngitis progressing to dry viral cough/bronchitic symptoms; overall mild-to-moderate and fluctuating over one week.
  - Plan:
    - Symptomatic care: paracetamol recommended (dose/route/frequency not documented), plenty of fluids, rest.
    - Sick note provided for additional time off work as requested.
    - Safety-netting: advise patient to seek in-person GP or urgent care if worsening or new concerning features occur (increasing or sudden change in breathlessness, persistent high fever, new hemoptysis, inability to ambulate or perform usual activities).
    - If symptoms not improving within expected timeframe (clinician estimated improvement over next 4–5 days), arrange in-person assessment.
- Issue 2: Possible viral-induced reactive airways disease / new-onset asthma
  - Assessment: New wheeze and exertional dyspnea temporally related to viral illness — plausible but unconfirmed.
  - Plan:
    - If wheeze or exertional breathlessness persists or recurs after acute illness resolves, recommend in-person assessment with auscultation and objective testing (peak flow or spirometry) and consideration of bronchodilator trial per primary care guidance.
    - Consider referral to primary care or respiratory clinic if recurrent or persistent symptoms.
- Issue 3: Atypical pneumonia / lower respiratory tract infection (less likely)
  - Assessment: Possible but less likely given overall mild course and lack of focal/systemic toxicity.
  - Plan:
    - If clinical status worsens, persistent fever, or failure to improve within expected timeframe, recommend in-person evaluation including chest auscultation and chest x-ray and consideration of empirical antibiotics if indicated by clinician on exam.
- General plan items:
  - Safety-netting reiterated: seek urgent care/GP promptly for increasing or sudden breathlessness, new chest pain worsening, hemoptysis, syncope, or inability to care for self.
  - Follow-up: return to care if not improving in ~4–5 days or sooner if symptoms worsen.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: No vitals recorded; no physical exam findings or lung auscultation documented; no investigations (CBC, CRP, chest x‑ray, or spirometry) performed or recorded.
- Conflicts / discrepancies:
  - Recorded DOB in transcript is 9 May 2016 (would indicate a child), but the consultation content (requesting sick note for work, adult social history) describes an adult — conflict noted.
  - No other major conflicts between transcript and provided DDx; DDx supports clinician impression (viral illness) and raises additional considerations (reactive airways, atypical pneumonia).
- Transcript quality: Consultation audio/transcript content clear and sufficient for history; limited by lack of physical exam and objective data.
